title: Mass Jewish Emigration from Iraq
description: The Iraqi government passed the Denaturalization Law, stripping citizenship from Jews who wished to emigrate. Approximately 120,000 Iraqi Jews departed for Israel in the early 1950s via Operation Ezra and Nehemiah airlifts, effectively ending one of the world's oldest Jewish communities and reshaping Baghdad's commercial and cultural landscape.

title: IPC Oil Royalties Renegotiated — 50/50 Profit Sharing
description: Iraq secured a 50-50 profit-sharing arrangement with the Iraq Petroleum Company consortium, increasing state income and funding infrastructure expansion. The IPC concession remained politically contentious, fueling nationalist demands for full nationalization.

title: November Uprising — Intifada of 1952
description: A popular uprising broke out in November driven by economic grievances, opposition to the British-backed monarchy, and anger at the Arab defeat in Palestine. The government declared martial law and cracked down on political parties, revealing deep tensions between the urban poor and the Hashemite establishment.

title: King Faisal II Assumes the Throne
description: King Faisal II formally assumed royal powers at age 18. Educated in England and considered Western-oriented, his reign was marked by tension between modernization and growing nationalist opposition to the monarchy.

title: Baghdad Development Board's Five-Year Plan
description: Iraq's Development Board launched an ambitious five-year plan financed by rising oil revenues, prioritizing dams, roads, ports, and public housing. Critics argued the plan favored urban elites and neglected rural poverty.

title: Iraq Joins the Baghdad Pact
description: Iraq signed the Baghdad Pact with Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, and the UK, creating a Cold War defense alliance to contain Soviet influence. It made Iraq the only Arab country aligned with a Western-led military organization and deepened the divide with Arab neighbors.

title: Suez Crisis Inflames Iraqi Public Opinion
description: Britain and France's invasion of Egypt following the Suez Canal nationalization caused mass protests in Baghdad. The crisis dramatically boosted pan-Arab nationalist sentiment and eroded the Hashemite monarchy's legitimacy.

title: 14 July Revolution — Monarchy Overthrown
description: Brigadier Abd al-Karim Qasim and Colonel Abd al-Salam Arif led a swift military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy, killing King Faisal II and Prime Minister Nuri al-Said. Iraq was proclaimed a republic and the Baghdad Pact repudiated, fundamentally reshaping Iraqi politics.

title: Agrarian Reform Law Issued
description: The new republican government issued a sweeping agrarian reform law redistributing large landholdings and placing ceilings on individual ownership, targeting the landowning class that had supported the monarchy.

title: Failed Ba'athist Assassination Attempt on Qasim
description: Ba'ath Party operatives ambushed Qasim's motorcade on October 7, wounding him but failing to kill him. Among the plotters was a young Saddam Hussein, who fled to Syria and Egypt after the attempt.

title: OPEC Founded with Iraqi Participation
description: Iraq was among the five founding members of OPEC, formed in Baghdad in September 1960, aimed at coordinating oil production and resisting unilateral price cuts by Western companies.

title: Kurdish Revolt Begins under Mustafa Barzani
description: General Mustafa Barzani launched a major armed uprising in September 1961 demanding Kurdish autonomy, with the KDP coordinating political direction. Iraqi army offensives were repulsed by peshmerga guerrillas, defining Iraq's northern politics for the next three decades.

title: Iraq Claims Kuwait at Independence
description: When Britain granted Kuwait independence, Qasim immediately claimed the emirate as an integral part of Iraq citing Ottoman precedents. Britain deployed troops to deter military action; the Arab League admitted Kuwait as a member and Iraq backed down, establishing a recurring territorial claim.

title: Ba'ath Party Seizes Power — Qasim Killed
description: On February 8, 1963, a Ba'ath Party-led coup overthrew and killed Qasim, reportedly with CIA intelligence assistance. The Ba'ath Party established the National Guard militia and immediately embarked on mass killings of communists.

title: Ba'athist Massacre of Iraqi Communists
description: Following the February coup, Ba'athist National Guard units conducted systematic raids executing hundreds of communist activists and intellectuals, reportedly using CIA-provided lists. The massacre effectively destroyed the Iraqi Communist Party's organizational capacity for years.

title: First Ba'ath Regime Collapses — Arif Takes Power
description: Internal Ba'ath divisions and the brutal National Guard militia led to a counter-coup in November 1963. President Abd al-Salam Arif ousted the Ba'athists after only nine months in power, demonstrating the party's political immaturity before its return in 1968.

title: Economic Nationalizations under Arif
description: President Arif nationalized major industries including banking, insurance, and large commercial companies following Egypt's socialist model, creating a large but inefficient public sector and causing capital flight.

title: Iraq in the Six-Day War
description: Iraq participated in the June 1967 Arab-Israeli War, sending armored and air units to support Jordan and Syria. The Arab defeat shattered pan-Arab nationalism and weakened the Arif government's legitimacy, energizing Ba'athist factions.

title: Ba'ath Party Returns to Power — July Revolution
description: On July 17, 1968, Ba'athist officers led by Ahmad Hasan al-Bakr overthrew Abd al-Rahman Arif. Two weeks later the Ba'athists purged non-Ba'athist partners. Saddam Hussein became deputy chairman and began building the security state that would define Ba'athist rule for 35 years.

title: March 1970 Manifesto — Kurdish Autonomy Agreement
description: The Ba'ath government and Mustafa Barzani reached the March 11 Manifesto promising Kurdish self-governance within four years, recognizing Kurdish as an official language in Kurdish areas. Both sides viewed it as temporary, and preparations for renewed conflict continued.

title: Nationalization of Iraq Petroleum Company
description: Iraq nationalized the IPC in June 1972 with Soviet technical assistance keeping production running. Oil revenues now fully accruing to the state surged after the 1973 oil shock, giving the Ba'ath government the financial foundation for social programs and military buildup.

title: Iraqi-Soviet Friendship Treaty Signed
description: Iraq signed a formal Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation with the Soviet Union, guaranteeing access to weapons, technical advisors, and diplomatic backing. The relationship gave Baghdad strategic depth against Israel and Iran.

title: Oil Price Shock — Revenue Windfall and Ba'ath Consolidation
description: The 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled global oil prices, generating an enormous revenue windfall for Iraq. Oil revenues funded rapid military expansion, social welfare, and industrialization, transforming Iraq's development trajectory but also financing future military adventurism.

title: Kurdish Autonomy Agreement Collapses — War Resumes
description: The 1970 March Manifesto deadline passed without genuine implementation. The Ba'ath offered a limited autonomy law excluding Kirkuk; Barzani rejected it and resumed armed resistance with massive Iranian support, erupting into the heaviest fighting since 1961.

title: Arabization and Mass Displacement of Kurds
description: The Iraqi government escalated Arabization policies in disputed border zones, forcibly displacing Kurdish and Turkmen villages and replacing residents with Arab settlers. Hundreds of thousands of Kurds were relocated, systematically engineering Kirkuk's ethnic composition and fueling generational grievances.

title: Algiers Accord — Iran Ends Kurdish Support
description: The Algiers Accord between Iraq and Iran resolved the Shatt al-Arab border dispute in exchange for Iran cutting off support to Barzani's movement. Deprived of supply lines the Kurdish revolt collapsed within weeks, representing a major diplomatic triumph for Saddam Hussein.

title: Ba'ath Literacy Campaign and Social Development
description: The Ba'ath government launched a national literacy campaign recognized by UNESCO, dramatically reducing adult illiteracy. Education, healthcare, and electricity were expanded across rural areas and women's workforce participation increased, legitimizing authoritarian rule through genuine social gains.

title: Shia Pilgrimage Protests — Safar Intifada
description: Tens of thousands of Shia pilgrims en route to Karbala clashed with security forces. The government executed eight Shia clerics and arrested hundreds, deepening sectarian tensions that would explode after the Iranian Revolution.

title: Saddam Hussein Becomes President — Ba'ath Purge
description: In July 1979, Saddam forced al-Bakr to resign and assumed the presidency, immediately reading out a list of alleged conspirators at a party congress. Twenty-two senior Ba'athists were executed by firing squad composed of their former colleagues, a calculated exercise in terror that paralyzed the party with fear.

title: Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr Executed
description: Saddam Hussein ordered the arrest and execution of Iraq's most prominent Shia scholar, Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, along with his sister. The killings sent a clear message to the Shia religious establishment about the limits of political Islam under Ba'athist rule.

title: Iran-Iraq War Begins
description: On September 22, 1980, Saddam Hussein launched a full-scale invasion of Iran, seeking to exploit post-revolutionary chaos and assert dominance over the Shatt al-Arab. Iraqi forces were slowed by fierce resistance after initial gains; the conflict became an eight-year war of attrition killing approximately one million people.

title: Israel Destroys Iraq's Osirak Nuclear Reactor
description: Israeli Air Force jets destroyed the French-built Osirak nuclear reactor near Baghdad on June 7, 1981 in Operation Opera, drawing broad international condemnation but effectively setting back Iraq's nuclear weapons program.

title: Chemical Weapons Deployed Against Iran
description: Iraq began deploying mustard gas and nerve agents against Iranian forces, becoming the first country since World War One to use chemical weapons on a large scale in combat. Western governments were aware but looked the other way given strategic interest in an Iranian defeat.

title: Barzani Clan Members Massacred
description: Saddam Hussein's forces arrested approximately 8,000 male members of the Barzani tribe and executed them in mass graves in the southern desert, an act of collective punishment foreshadowing the Anfal genocide.

title: Tanker War in the Persian Gulf
description: Iraq began attacking Iranian oil tankers and shipping in the Gulf to pressure Iran economically. Iran retaliated against ships serving Gulf Arab states. Hundreds of civilian ships were damaged or sunk, drawing US naval forces to protect shipping lanes.

title: War of the Cities — Missile Strikes on Civilian Populations
description: Iraq launched Scud missile attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities; Iran responded with its own strikes on Baghdad and Basra. The exchanges caused significant civilian casualties and mass evacuations, demonstrating both sides' willingness to target civilian populations.

title: Iraq's War Economy and Alternative Oil Routes
description: Iraq developed alternative oil export routes through Turkey and Saudi Arabia as the Gulf war zone threatened the Basra terminal. Despite war pressures, Iraq continued social spending financed by Gulf Arab loans, accumulating over $80 billion in war debt that would create severe postwar economic stress.

title: Iran Captures Faw Peninsula
description: Iran's amphibious assault in February 1986 captured the Faw Peninsula, threatening Basra and representing a major strategic blow to Iraq. The Faw loss galvanized Iraqi use of chemical weapons more aggressively to change battlefield outcomes.

title: Halabja Chemical Massacre
description: On March 16-17, 1988, Iraqi aircraft dropped chemical weapons on the Kurdish town of Halabja, killing between 3,200 and 5,000 civilians immediately with thousands more dying from long-term effects. It was the largest chemical weapons attack against a civilian population in history.

title: Anfal Genocide Against Iraqi Kurds
description: The Ba'ath government launched the Anfal military campaign from February to September 1988, systematically targeting Kurdish civilians with chemical weapons, artillery, and ground troops. An estimated 4,000 villages were destroyed and 50,000 to 182,000 Kurds killed, constituting genocide under international law.

title: Iran-Iraq War Ends with UN Ceasefire
description: Iran accepted UN Security Council Resolution 598 on July 18, 1988, ending the eight-year war. Over one million lives were lost, leaving hundreds of thousands disabled and both economies devastated. Iraq emerged with the Arab world's largest military but over $80 billion in debt.

title: Post-War Economic Crisis and Kuwait Tensions
description: Iraq faced acute economic crisis after the war with over $80 billion in external debt. Saddam pushed Gulf Arab creditors, especially Kuwait, for debt relief. Kuwait's refusal and alleged slant-drilling into the Rumaila oilfield became major grievances leading to the 1990 invasion.

title: Iraq Invades and Annexes Kuwait
description: On August 2, 1990, Iraqi forces overran Kuwait in hours and Saddam announced its annexation as Iraq's 19th province. The UN Security Council passed Resolution 660 demanding immediate withdrawal and the US began assembling a broad international coalition to reverse the conquest.

title: UN Comprehensive Sanctions Imposed on Iraq
description: The UN Security Council imposed comprehensive economic sanctions via Resolution 661 on August 6, 1990, cutting off oil exports and most imports. The sanctions, maintained after the Gulf War through the 1990s, devastated Iraq's civilian population with soaring infant mortality and malnutrition.

title: Gulf War — Operation Desert Storm
description: A US-led coalition of 35 nations launched Operation Desert Storm on January 17, 1991, with massive air strikes followed by a ground campaign that routed Iraqi forces in Kuwait in 100 hours. Kuwait was liberated and Saddam accepted ceasefire terms but retained power in Baghdad.

title: Shia and Kurdish Uprisings Crushed — 1991 Intifada
description: Spontaneous uprisings erupted across southern Iraq and the Kurdish north after Iraq's defeat, but US forces stood aside as Saddam's Republican Guard crushed the southern rebellion with extreme brutality, killing an estimated 30,000-60,000 Shias in the south and some 20,000 Kurds in the north.

title: Kurdish Refugee Crisis and Northern No-Fly Zone
description: Republican Guard suppression of the Kurdish uprising caused over one million Kurds to flee toward Turkey and Iran. The US, UK, and France established a no-fly zone (Operation Provide Comfort) on April 6, 1991, creating a safe haven that enabled the de facto Kurdish autonomous region.

title: Kurdish Regional Government Established
description: With protection from the northern no-fly zone, Iraqi Kurdistan held elections on May 19, 1992 and established a Kurdistan Regional Government. KDP and PUK shared power in three northern provinces effectively expelled from Baghdad's authority.

title: Oil-for-Food Program Negotiations Begin
description: Iraq and the UN continued negotiations on a program allowing limited oil sales to fund humanitarian imports while maintaining broader sanctions. The UN first proposed such a mechanism via Resolution 706 in 1991, but Iraq initially declined; the formal Oil-for-Food program was established by Resolution 986 in April 1995. The human cost of comprehensive sanctions mounted throughout this period, with UNICEF documenting dramatically elevated child mortality rates.

title: Intra-Kurdish Civil War
description: The Kurdish Regional Government collapsed into civil war between the KDP and PUK on May 1, 1994, fighting over revenue sharing and political power. The KDP received military backing from Saddam in 1996 to capture Erbil. The conflict caused an estimated 5,000-8,000 casualties and was eventually resolved by the 1998 Washington Agreement.

title: UNSCOM Discovers Full Extent of Biological Weapons Program
description: UN inspectors made a breakthrough when Saddam's son-in-law Hussein Kamel defected in August 1995, after which Iraq was forced to reveal its biological weapons program had weaponized anthrax, botulinum toxin, and aflatoxin on an industrial scale. Kamel returned to Iraq in February 1996 and was killed shortly after.

title: Oil-for-Food Program Begins Operating
description: Iraq accepted UN Resolution 986 and signed a memorandum of understanding in May 1996, with the first oil exports beginning in December 1996. The program generated over $64 billion before closure in 2003 but was plagued by massive corruption with Iraqi officials and international contractors skimming billions.

title: Operation Desert Fox — US-UK Air Strikes
description: After UNSCOM inspectors reported Iraqi non-cooperation in December 1998, the US and UK launched Operation Desert Fox from December 16-19, a campaign of over 600 sorties and 415 cruise missiles against Iraqi military and government targets. Iraq declared the UN weapons inspection regime over and refused future inspections.

title: Grand Ayatollah al-Sadr II Assassinated
description: Grand Ayatollah Muhammad Sadiq al-Sadr was assassinated along with two sons on February 19, 1999, while driving in Najaf. The Shia community erupted in violently suppressed protests, making al-Sadr a martyr figure whose movement was later revived by his son Muqtada al-Sadr after 2003.

title: 9/11 Aftermath and Iraq in US War Planning
description: Despite no proven connection to September 11, the Bush administration began planning military action against Saddam Hussein by late 2001. On November 21, 2001, Bush directed Rumsfeld to begin planning for war with Iraq. Neoconservative officials argued removing Saddam was essential to regional transformation, and intelligence agencies were pressed to find Iraq-al-Qaeda connections.

title: UN Weapons Inspectors Return — UNMOVIC
description: Under intense US pressure and UN Security Council Resolution 1441, Iraq agreed to allow UN inspectors to return under UNMOVIC in November 2002. Chief inspector Hans Blix found no confirmed WMD stockpiles; the US and UK argued Iraq was deceiving inspectors while France and Russia said inspections should continue.

title: US-Led Invasion of Iraq — Operation Iraqi Freedom
description: On March 20, 2003, a US-led coalition invaded Iraq without UN Security Council authorization. Baghdad fell on April 9, Saddam's government collapsed, and no WMDs were found. The invasion unleashed sectarian conflict, insurgency, and regional instability transforming the Middle East for decades.

title: De-Ba'athification and Army Dissolution
description: Coalition Provisional Authority chief Paul Bremer issued CPA Order 1 (de-Ba'athification, May 16) and CPA Order 2 (dissolution of the Iraqi Army, May 23) in 2003. The decisions put approximately 400,000 military personnel out of work, creating a massive insurgency recruitment pool and removing administrators needed to run a functioning state.

title: Saddam Hussein Captured
description: US forces captured Saddam Hussein on December 13, 2003, in a spider hole near ad-Dawr, south of Tikrit, in Operation Red Dawn. His capture raised hopes the insurgency might abate but violence continued to escalate. He was later transferred to Iraqi custody for trial before the Iraqi High Tribunal.

title: Abu Ghraib Prison Abuse Scandal
description: Photographs of US military personnel abusing Iraqi detainees at Abu Ghraib were broadcast by CBS on April 28, 2004, causing international outrage. The scandal severely damaged American credibility and was exploited by insurgent groups for recruitment. Eleven soldiers were convicted at court-martial but higher command responsibility was largely avoided.

title: Battles of Fallujah and Sovereignty Transfer
description: Two major coalition assaults on Fallujah -- an insurgent stronghold -- and transfer of nominal sovereignty to an Iraqi interim government under Ayad Allawi on June 28, 2004 marked pivotal occupation milestones. The Second Battle of Fallujah (Operation Phantom Fury, November 7) became the most intense urban combat for US forces since Hue in 1968, while real authority remained with US forces.

title: Iraqi Elections, Constitution, and Shia Political Dominance
description: Iraq held historic parliamentary elections on January 30, 2005, with the United Iraqi Alliance winning 48% of the vote amid Sunni boycott. A new constitution was ratified in the October 15 referendum with 78.6% approval, establishing a federal parliamentary republic with Islam as legislative foundation. Both events confirmed Shia political dominance after decades of Ba'athist rule, deepening Sunni alienation.

title: Samarra Shrine Bombing Triggers Sectarian Civil War
description: The bombing of the al-Askari shrine in Samarra on February 22, 2006, one of Shia Islam's holiest sites, triggered an explosion of sectarian violence. Over 100 bodies were found the next day and well over 1,000 killed in the following days. Baghdad descended into tit-for-tat killings and ethnic cleansing killing tens of thousands and displacing over two million people internally.

title: Saddam Hussein Executed
description: Saddam Hussein was convicted of crimes against humanity for the 1982 Dujail massacre and executed by hanging on December 30, 2006, at Camp Justice in Baghdad. The execution on Eid al-Adha, accompanied by sectarian taunting broadcast worldwide via mobile phone footage, was itself controversial and reinforced Sunni grievances.

title: US Troop Surge and Sunni Awakening
description: In January 2007, President Bush deployed 30,000 additional troops under General Petraeus with a new counterinsurgency strategy, bringing US troop strength to 165,000. Simultaneously, the Sunni Awakening saw tribal leaders turn against al-Qaeda in Iraq; the Sons of Iraq movement eventually encompassed over 100,000 fighters. Violence dropped dramatically by late 2007.

title: Battle of Basra and US-Iraq Status of Forces Agreement
description: Prime Minister Maliki led a military operation against the Mahdi Army in Basra in March 2008, asserting central government authority. The Status of Forces Agreement, ratified by parliament in November 2008 and effective from January 1, 2009, set a timeline for full US troop withdrawal by December 31, 2011, representing a major assertion of Iraqi sovereignty.

title: Maliki Consolidates Sectarian Governance
description: Prime Minister Maliki's government increasingly governed along Shia sectarian lines, sidelining Sunni politicians, targeting Sunni leaders with terrorism accusations, and conducting mass arrests of Sunni citizens. His centralization of security forces and sectarian favoritism created the alienation that enabled ISIS to find active Sunni support.

title: Iraqi Parliamentary Elections and Nine-Month Deadlock
description: Iraq held elections on March 7, 2010, with Ayad Allawi's Iraqiya coalition winning 91 seats (narrow plurality over Maliki's 89), but Maliki refused to accept defeat. Eight to nine months of political deadlock followed before a second Maliki term was confirmed on December 22, 2010, under a power-sharing agreement that was never genuinely implemented.

title: US Forces Complete Withdrawal from Iraq
description: The last 500 US combat troops withdrew from Iraq on the morning of December 18, 2011, ending nearly nine years of military presence. The war left nearly 4,500 American soldiers dead and tens of thousands of Iraqis killed. The Iraqi military was not fully capable of maintaining security, and Maliki's government was moving in an increasingly sectarian and authoritarian direction.

title: ISIS Exploits Syrian Civil War to Rebuild
description: The Syrian Civil War created ungoverned territory that the Islamic State of Iraq exploited to expand, recruiting fighters and accessing new weapons. Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi extended operations into Syria, establishing Jabhat al-Nusra in January 2012, and between July 2012 and July 2013 carried out 24 waves of car bomb attacks and 8 prison breaks in Iraq. In April 2013 he formally announced the creation of ISIS.

title: Hawija Massacre and Sunni Insurgency Revival
description: Iraqi security forces' assault on a Sunni protest camp in Hawija on April 23, 2013 killed 42 people and injured at least 153, ending Sunni hopes for peaceful political change. The subsequent violence killed over 300 in the following days. Car bombings and sectarian attacks escalated sharply throughout 2013, with over 9,000 Iraqi civilians killed that year -- the highest toll since 2007-2008.

title: ISIS Captures Mosul and Declares Caliphate
description: Between June 4-10, 2014, approximately 3,000 ISIS fighters routed up to 60,000 Iraqi Army and police forces and captured Mosul. On June 29, ISIS declared a global caliphate with al-Baghdadi as caliph from Mosul's Great Mosque, controlling territory spanning Iraq and Syria and occupying 40% of Iraq's territory.

title: Yazidi Genocide on Sinjar Mountain
description: ISIS attacked the Yazidi population of Sinjar on August 3, 2014, massacring men and boys and enslaving women and girls after Peshmerga forces withdrew. An estimated 5,000 Yazidis were killed and 7,000 enslaved in what the UN classified as genocide. Nearly 200,000 Yazidis fled toward Mount Sinjar. The atrocity shocked the world into renewed international intervention.

title: Maliki Replaced by Haider al-Abadi; US-Led Coalition Launches Airstrikes
description: Under US and Iranian pressure, Maliki stepped down on August 14, 2014; Haider al-Abadi was confirmed as prime minister by parliament on September 8. In September, Obama announced a new international coalition launching airstrikes against ISIS in Iraq and Syria, with US special forces returning as advisors.

title: Counter-ISIS Campaign — Tikrit Retaken; ISIS at Peak Territorial Control
description: A force of 20,000-30,000 Iraqi troops and Iran-sponsored Popular Mobilization Forces, backed by US air power, launched the operation to recapture Tikrit on March 2, 2015, declaring it liberated on April 12. At its peak ISIS controlled approximately one-third of Iraq including major cities and oilfields, operating as a proto-state with taxes, courts, and utilities while destroying irreplaceable Assyrian sites at Nimrud and Hatra.

title: Battle of Fallujah and PMF Institutionalization
description: Iraqi forces and PMF launched Operation Breaking Terrorism on May 22, liberating Fallujah from ISIS by June 26, 2016. The Iraqi parliament passed legislation in November formalizing the Popular Mobilization Forces as an official security component, approved by President Masum on December 19, institutionalizing over 100,000 Iran-linked fighters within the Iraqi state.

title: Battle of Mosul — ISIS Territorial Defeat Declared
description: The nine-month battle to retake Mosul began October 16, 2016, with eastern Mosul liberated on January 24, 2017, and the western campaign beginning February 19. Prime Minister Abadi declared victory in Mosul on July 10, 2017. It was the most destructive urban combat of the 21st century, killing over 10,000 ISIS fighters and tens of thousands of civilians.

title: Kurdistan Independence Referendum Backfires
description: KRG President Barzani held an independence referendum on September 25, 2017, winning 92.73% support, but Baghdad, Iran, Turkey, and the US all opposed it. On October 15, Iraqi forces and PMF seized Kirkuk without significant resistance. The independence bid collapsed, Barzani resigned on November 1, and the KRG lost 40% of its territory and its main revenue source.

title: Post-ISIS Elections and Iran-Backed Parties Win
description: Parliamentary elections on May 12, 2018 produced a fragmented result with Muqtada al-Sadr's Sairoon alliance winning 54 seats (largest bloc) and Iran-backed Fatah Alliance (Hadi al-Amiri) second. Coalition building took months, resulting in Adil Abdul-Mahdi confirmed as prime minister in October 2018 in a compromise arrangement.

title: Basra Protests Over Services and Contaminated Water
description: Mass protests erupted in Basra in July-September 2018 over contaminated water supplies, power cuts, unemployment, and corrupt governance. Over 118,000 people were hospitalized from contaminated water; protesters burned government buildings, Iranian consulates, and party offices. At least 15 were killed in clashes. A harbinger of the 2019 national uprising.

title: Post-ISIS Reconstruction Crisis and Displacement
description: Iraq faced colossal reconstruction challenges with Mosul, Fallujah, Ramadi, and Sinjar in ruins and millions of internally displaced persons. At the February 2018 Kuwait conference, international pledges of $30 billion were far below the $88.2 billion estimated need, with $22 billion needed in the short term alone. Reconstruction was severely hampered by corruption in contracting.

title: October Revolution — Mass Anti-Government Uprising
description: On October 25, 2019, the largest protest movement in post-2003 Iraqi history erupted in Baghdad and across southern Iraq (the Tishreen movement), demanding an end to corruption, sectarian governance, and Iranian interference. Security forces and Iran-backed militias killed some 600 protesters and injured over 20,000. The uprising forced Prime Minister Abdul-Mahdi to resign on November 29 and represented a generational rejection of the post-2003 political order.

title: Systematic Assassination of Protest Activists
description: Iran-backed militias conducted a campaign of targeted assassinations against protest organizers, activists, journalists, and social media personalities throughout 2019-2020. The UN documented 49 attempted assassinations and 72 kidnappings of activists between October 2019 and January 2020 alone. Hundreds were killed or abducted to terrorize the protest movement into submission.

title: US Kills Soleimani at Baghdad Airport
description: A US drone strike near Baghdad International Airport on January 3, 2020 killed Iranian Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani and Iraqi PMF deputy chairman Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, along with eight others. The Iraqi parliament voted to expel US forces; Iran launched missile strikes on US bases in Iraq, injuring dozens of American troops.

title: Mustafa al-Kadhimi Becomes Prime Minister
description: Former intelligence chief Mustafa al-Kadhimi was confirmed as prime minister by parliament on May 6, 2020, after two previous nominees failed during five months of political deadlock. He attempted a balancing act between the US and Iran while managing protest demands and collapsing oil revenues from COVID-19's impact on global energy markets.

title: Iraqi Elections — Record Low Turnout Amid Political Crisis
description: Parliamentary elections on October 10, 2021 saw a record low turnout of approximately 41%. Muqtada al-Sadr's movement won the largest bloc with 73 seats while Iran-backed Coordination Framework parties lost ground. Losing parties refused to accept results, alleging fraud, triggering prolonged political deadlock.

title: Government Formation Deadlock and Green Zone Clashes
description: Iraq experienced a 382-day government formation crisis. After Sadrist MPs resigned in June 2022, Sadrist supporters stormed the Green Zone on July 27 and August 29, with armed clashes killing at least 15 on August 29. Muqtada al-Sadr stood down, enabling Iran-backed Coordination Framework to complete government formation with Mohammed Shia al-Sudani confirmed as prime minister on October 27, 2022.

title: Iraq's Regional Diplomacy — Saudi-Iranian Rapprochement
description: Iraq played a foundational role in the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement, having hosted five rounds of reconciliation talks between Riyadh and Tehran during 2021-2022 under PM al-Kadhimi. The process culminated in a China-brokered agreement on March 10, 2023, to restore diplomatic relations after a seven-year hiatus. Iraq's bridging role reflected its unique geopolitical position between Gulf Arab states and Iran.

title: Kurdistan Oil Dispute — Turkey Halts Pipeline Exports
description: An ICC arbitration ruling issued February 13, 2023 ordered Turkey to pay Iraq over $1.5 billion for unauthorized oil exports from Iraqi Kurdistan between 2014 and 2018, prompting Turkey to halt the Ceyhan pipeline. The dispute triggered an acute fiscal crisis in Erbil and highlighted unresolved Baghdad-Erbil oil revenue tensions.

title: Severe Drought and Water Crisis in Southern Iraq
description: Iraq experienced its driest conditions on record since 1933, with the Tigris and Euphrates at historically low levels -- water levels dropped by up to 70% compared to prior years -- due to upstream Turkish and Iranian dam construction combined with climate change. Iraq receives less than 35% of its theoretical water share. Southern marshlands faced ecological collapse, agricultural output fell sharply, and the water crisis was identified as a major long-term national security threat.

title: US-Iran Proxy Tensions on Iraqi Soil Escalate
description: Iran-backed militia groups conducted over 160 drone and rocket attacks on US bases in Iraq and Syria following the Gaza conflict's outbreak in October 2023. On January 28, 2024, a strike on Tower 22 in Jordan killed three US soldiers. The US launched retaliatory strikes on February 2 hitting 85 targets, and on February 7 killed a Kataib Hezbollah commander in Baghdad, triggering a political crisis.

title: Iraq Negotiates US Troop Withdrawal
description: Iraq opened formal negotiations with the US in January 2024 on withdrawal of international coalition combat forces. After six months of talks, a preliminary agreement was reached: hundreds of troops to leave by September 2025, with the remainder departing by the end of 2026. Al-Sudani faced domestic pressure from Iran-backed parties demanding US departure while needing American security assistance against ISIS.

title: Yazidi Survivors Begin Return to Sinjar
description: A decade after ISIS's genocide, 130,000-150,000 Yazidis returned to Sinjar amid pressure from Baghdad to close IDP camps in Kurdistan, though 80% of public infrastructure and 70% of homes remained in ruins. Thousands of Yazidis remained unaccounted for; Sinjar remained contested between Iraqi government forces, PMF, Kurdish Peshmerga, and PKK-linked groups.

title: Iraq's Economic Diversification Efforts
description: Iraq advanced the $17 billion Development Road project to transform Iraq into a transport hub connecting the Gulf to Europe via Turkey, and the World Bank approved a $930 million railway modernization project. Oil still comprised 99% of exports, with the rentier state model deeply entrenched despite reform rhetoric and PM al-Sudani's vision to transition to a diversified economy.

title: Al-Nuri Mosque and Its Minaret Reopen in Mosul After ISIS Destruction
description: Iraq reopened the reconstructed Great Mosque of al-Nuri in Mosul on 1 September 2025, eight years after Islamic State militants destroyed the 12th-century mosque and its leaning minaret in June 2017 as they lost control of the city. UNESCO led the roughly $115 million reconstruction, with major funding from the United Arab Emirates and the European Union, using traditional techniques and salvaged rubble to rebuild the nearly 850-year-old minaret. The project involved Iraqi heritage authorities and Sunni religious leaders in restoring a site of deep symbolic importance to Mosul's identity.
